title: Functions
summary: Declare and define functions, pass arguments and return values, overload by parameter type, supply default arguments, and move work to compile time with constexpr.
introduction: A function names a piece of work so you can call it from anywhere, test it on its own and read the program at a higher level. C++ functions add a few ideas that scripting languages lack: a declaration can be separated from its definition, several functions may share a name as long as their parameter types differ, and a `constexpr` function can run inside the compiler. This lesson covers all of that with programs you can compile as you go.
learningObjectives: Separate a function's declaration from its definition and explain why the order matters
Overload functions and predict which overload a call selects
Use default arguments and the [[nodiscard]] attribute
Write a constexpr function and check it with static_assert

blocks.text: A **declaration** (also called a prototype) states the return type, the name and the parameter types: `int square(int x);`. A **definition** adds the body. The compiler reads a file from top to bottom and must see at least a declaration before any call, which is why headers are full of declarations and `.cpp` files hold the definitions. Inside one file you can declare first and define later, as below.

blocks.title: average.cpp

blocks.text: `square` takes its argument **by value**: `x` is a copy, and changing it inside the function would not touch the caller's variable. `average` takes a `const std::vector<int>&`, a reference to the caller's vector, so nothing is copied and the `const` promises not to modify it. The [next lesson](/tutorials/cpp/references-pointers) explains references in depth; for now, pass small things (numbers, `char`, `bool`) by value and anything bigger by `const&`.

A function that returns nothing has the return type `void`. `return;` with no value leaves it early. Every non-`void` function must return a value on every path; forgetting one is undefined behaviour, and `-Wall` reports it as `control reaches end of non-void function`.

Several functions may share a name if their parameter lists differ; the compiler picks the best match from the argument types at each call. This is **overloading**, and it is how `std::cout << x` works for every type. A parameter can also carry a **default argument**, used when the caller omits it; defaults must come last and are written in the declaration.

blocks.title: overload.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra overload.cpp -o overload
$ ./overload
int 7
double 7.5
string "seven"
Hello, Ada!
Welcome back, Ada!

blocks.text: Overload resolution prefers an exact match, then standard conversions (`int` to `double`), then user-defined conversions (a string literal to `std::string`). Two overloads that differ only in return type are not allowed, because the return type plays no part in choosing.

Marking a function `constexpr` allows the compiler to evaluate it while compiling, whenever the arguments are known constants. The same function still works with run-time values. `static_assert` turns that into a test that fails the build instead of a test that fails at night.

blocks.title: factorial.cpp

blocks.text: `factorial` calls itself: that is **recursion**, and it needs a base case (`n <= 1`) or it would never stop. The return type is `long long` because `13!` already overflows a 32-bit `int`, and signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C++, not a wrap-around.

When a function's only purpose is its result, mark it `[[nodiscard]]`; the compiler then warns if a caller throws the result away, which usually means a forgotten `if`. The trailing form `auto name(params) -> type` is equivalent to writing the type first and is common in generic code where the return type depends on the parameters.

blocks.title: leap.cpp
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra leap.cpp -o leap
leap.cpp: In function 'int main()':
leap.cpp:16:11: warning: ignoring return value of 'bool isLeap(int)', declared with attribute 'nodiscard' [-Wunused-result]
   16 |     isLeap(2024);   // result ignored: the compiler warns
      |     ~~~~~~^~~~~~
$ ./leap
1900: 365
2000: 366
2024: 366
2026: 365

blocks.text: The exact wording and column number of the warning vary between compiler versions, but the program still builds; a warning never stops the build unless you pass `-Werror`.

blocks.title: Common mistake: calling before declaring
blocks.text: Move `main` to the top of a file and define `square` below it without the prototype, and GCC stops with `error: 'square' was not declared in this scope`. C++ does not look ahead the way JavaScript hoists functions or Python resolves names at call time. Either define functions before `main` or keep the declarations at the top (or in a header) and define in any order.

blocks.title: Keep functions short and pure where you can
blocks.text: A function that takes its inputs as parameters, returns its result and touches no global state is easy to test, easy to reuse and safe to call from several threads. Reserve `void` functions with side effects for the edges of your program: printing, writing files, talking to hardware.

questions.question: Given `void show(int)` and `void show(double)`, which overload does `show(3.0f)` call?
questions.explanation: `3.0f` is a `float`. Converting it to `double` is a promotion, which ranks above the conversion to `int`, so the `double` overload wins.
options: The call is ambiguous and does not compile

questions.question: A `constexpr` function can only be called with arguments known at compile time.
questions.explanation: `constexpr` permits compile-time evaluation but does not require it. The same function works with run-time values such as input from `std::cin`.
